plan.topic: Fatigue on tirzepatide: how often it was reported (Zepbound label: 5%, 6% and 7% by dose vs 3% on placebo, pooled SURMOUNT-1 and -2), likely everyday contributors (eating much less, low fluids, too little protein, poor sleep, GI side effects), and when tiredness is a reason to call the prescriber
plan.angle:
Lane A (log 'lane: A'; publisher adds it to the 'Life on Tirzepatide' playlist). Runs 8–12 min at 14:00 ET.

The first spoken sentence answers the title: 'Tiredness is a listed side effect of tirzepatide, but it was uncommon in the trials: about 5 to 7 in 100 people across doses, versus 3 in 100 on placebo.' Then a 'you' scenario: it's November, the days are shorter, you're eating far less, and you're dragging by 3 pm. One seasonal line in the intro at most. The body rests on the label, the NHS tiredness pages (2023) and the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory.

Chapters, named as searched questions:
(1) Is fatigue a side effect of tirzepatide? Give the label's per-dose rates vs placebo exactly as printed, with the pooled-trial population. Write the narration numbers as words and check every one in speech-to-text.
(2) Why might you feel tired? Possible contributors, each worded 'can' and never as proven cause: eating much less, low fluids, skipped protein, poor sleep, and nausea or diarrhoea. The general causes come from NHS, tagged NHS.
(3) Could it be dehydration? Use the label's dehydration and kidney wording exactly. Sipping fluids, unless you've been told to limit them, is our own tip with no tag.
(4) Does protein help energy? Credit only what the advisory says (getting enough protein). The kidney caveat goes in.
(5) What about sleep and movement? General guidance only. Strength training follows the advisory's exact wording, started gently.
(6) Could something else be going on? Questions for your clinician, including whether blood tests (e.g. iron, thyroid) make sense. No supplement promises.
(7) When should you call your prescriber? Dizziness or fainting, vomiting or diarrhoea with signs of dehydration, and, for people who also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, low blood sugar signs, all in label wording.

Format and safety rules:
- Re-hook every 45–75 s.
- One subscribe ask, after the chapter 2–4 'what helps' payoff.
- No dosing or titration content. Never say 'adjust your dose'.
- Include 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own', one GI line, 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Each must be both spoken and in the on-screen field.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' No spoken titles. The publisher links Side Effects or What to Eat.
- Thumbnail: a state change from drained to recharged, 4 words or fewer, not reusing title words (e.g. 'Running on Empty?' → answered). One labelled character, calm mood, no body imagery.

scenes.narration: If that's you, you're not imagining it, and you're not failing at anything. Tiredness is real, and it usually has reasons you can actually look at.

scenes.section: Is fatigue a side effect of tirzepatide?

scenes.section: Is fatigue a side effect of tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: And notice something. Three in a hundred people reported fatigue on a dummy injection. Life, sleep and stress don't pause for a clinical trial.

scenes.section: Is fatigue a side effect of tirzepatide?
scenes.narration: That's the fact. But it doesn't tell you why some people feel drained. And here's where it gets interesting, because the likely reasons are things you can look at.
So, why might you feel tired?
Let's bring someone in. Imagine Priya, forty-four, a teacher, four months into tirzepatide. Food feels quieter, which she likes. But by mid-afternoon she's running on fumes.

visual.stock_query: hypothetical teacher tired at classroom desk

scenes.narration: The NHS lists the usual everyday drivers of tiredness: not getting enough sleep, an unhealthy diet, not enough exercise, and stress.
On tirzepatide, a few of these can stack up in ways that are easy to miss. Here are five.
One. Eating much less. Tirzepatide reduces appetite and food intake, which is part of how it works. But less food means less fuel, and that can leave you feeling flat.

visual.stock_query: small plate, fuel gauge near empty

scenes.narration: The NHS suggests eating regular meals and healthy snacks every three to four hours, rather than a large meal less often. With a quiet appetite, small and regular may feel easier anyway.
Two. Low fluids. When you eat less, you also miss the water that comes with food. And if you're not thirsty, it's easy to drink less too.
Three. Too little protein. When your plate shrinks, protein often shrinks with it. We'll come back to why that matters.

visual.stock_query: shrinking plate with tiny protein portion

scenes.narration: Four. Poor sleep. Dark evenings, late nights, a racing mind. Sleep affects energy for everyone, medicine or not.

visual.stock_query: person awake in bed, phone glow

scenes.narration: And five. Nausea or diarrhoea. If your stomach's unsettled, you may eat and drink less, and you can lose fluids too. That can add up to feeling wiped out.

A quick word on those stomach symptoms. Nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation are among the most common side effects on the label. If they're making it hard to eat or drink, tell your prescriber.
Notice the word 'can' in all of this. None of these is proven to be the cause of your tiredness. They're simply sensible places to look first.
For Priya, it's probably a bit of several. But one of them is the easiest to miss, and it's the one we'll check first.
Could it be dehydration?
The NHS puts it plainly: sometimes you're tired simply because you're mildly dehydrated.
On tirzepatide, fluids matter for another reason. The patient guide in the label says diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids, called dehydration, which may cause kidney problems.
The label also says it's important to drink fluids to help reduce your chance of dehydration.
So how do you know if you're running low? The NHS lists signs like feeling thirsty, dark yellow, strong-smelling pee, peeing less often, feeling dizzy or lightheaded, a dry mouth, and feeling tired.
Here's a ten-second check you can do today. The NHS suggests drinking enough during the day that your pee is a pale colour.

visual.stock_query: pale to dark yellow colour chart

scenes.narration: One simple habit: keep a bottle within reach and sip through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids.

visual.stock_query: water bottle on desk, smiling mascot

scenes.narration: Priya tries it. By the end of the week, her afternoon slump feels a little softer. Not gone. Softer. Because fluids were only part of her story.
The next part is about her plate. And it's not about eating more. It's about what she makes sure is on it.
Does protein help energy?

In twenty twenty-five, four groups, the American College of Lifestyle Medicine, the American Society for Nutrition, the Obesity Medicine Association and The Obesity Society, published a joint advisory on nutrition for people on GLP-1 medicines.
One of its clearest messages: get enough protein. When you're eating much less, protein helps preserve muscle while you lose weight.
Now, the honest bit. The advisory doesn't claim protein cures tiredness. Its point is that when your intake drops, protein is one thing not to let slip.
The practical version: build each small meal around a protein. Eggs, yoghurt, fish, chicken, beans or tofu. Start there, then add the rest.
One caveat. If you have kidney disease, your protein needs may be different, so ask your clinician what amount suits you.
So that's three possible drains, and three things you can try today: small, regular meals, steady sips, and protein first on the plate.
If that was useful, we answer one tirzepatide question from the research every day. Subscribe, and the next answer comes to you.
But food and fluids are only half the energy story. The other half happens while you sleep, and when you move. And the movement advice may feel backwards at first.

visual.stock_query: moon and sneaker side by side

scenes.narration: What about sleep and movement?

visual.stock_query: chapter card, pillow and walking shoe

scenes.narration: Start with sleep. The CDC says most adults need at least seven hours a night. If you're regularly getting less, that alone can leave you foggy.

visual.stat_label: Sleep most adults need nightly, per CDC

scenes.narration: The NHS tips are simple. Go to bed and get up at the same time every day, try to avoid naps in the day, and take time to relax before bed.

Caffeine is a sneaky one. The NHS says it can disrupt your sleep and leave you tired in the day, and its effects can last up to seven hours. If you want to cut back, do it gradually, because stopping suddenly can bring on headaches and trouble sleeping.
Now, movement. When you're exhausted, moving can feel like the last thing you want. But the NHS says even a fifteen-minute walk can give you an energy boost.
The GLP-1 advisory goes further. It recommends strength training at least three times a week, to help preserve muscle.
If that sounds like a lot right now, start gently. A few sit-to-stands from a chair. Wall push-ups. Light bands. Build from there, and check with your clinician if you have health conditions.
Back to Priya. She swaps late-night scrolling for an earlier bedtime and takes a short walk at lunch. Most days feel better. But one week, they don't. And that's when the next question matters.

visual.stock_query: teacher walking at lunch, then pausing

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: Tiredness has plenty of causes that have nothing to do with tirzepatide. The NHS lists conditions like iron deficiency anaemia, diabetes, an overactive thyroid and sleep apnoea, along with stress, low mood and life's challenges.

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: So it's reasonable to ask your clinician whether blood tests, for example for anaemia, diabetes or thyroid problems, make sense for you. That's their call to make with you, not a supplement aisle's.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask: are blood tests worth it?

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: And here's a twist. Sleep apnoea is a known cause of tiredness. And Zepbound is FDA-approved to treat moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with obesity.
scenes.retention_device: But here's where it gets weird

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: So if you snore loudly, wake up gasping, or never feel rested, say so. It's useful information for your clinician either way.

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: Other things worth mentioning: any other medicines you take, how your mood has been, and how much you're really eating and drinking. A few days of quick notes can make that conversation much easier.
scenes.on_screen_text: Bring a few days of notes

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: And please, don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own. If tiredness is bothering you, that's a conversation, not a solo decision.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own

visual.stock_query: calm mascot pointing to clinic door

scenes.section: Could something else be going on?
scenes.narration: So when does tiredness stop being a mention-it-next-time thing, and become a call-today thing? That's the last piece.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: When should you call your prescriber?

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: First, vomiting or diarrhoea with signs of dehydration. The label links that fluid loss to kidney problems, so if you can't keep fluids up, call your prescriber.

visual.stock_query: person on phone with water glass

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: The NHS says to get an urgent GP appointment or call one-one-one if you feel unusually tired, feel dizzy when you stand up and it doesn't go away, have dark yellow pee or are peeing less than normal, or are breathing quickly or have a fast heart rate. And if you're dehydrated and confused, or much sleepier than normal, call nine-nine-nine or your local emergency number.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Second, dizziness or fainting. Feeling faint, or actually passing out, is a reason to get checked promptly, not to push through.

visual.stock_query: person sitting down, calling for help

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Third, if you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, watch for low blood sugar. The label says your risk may be higher when tirzepatide is used with those medicines.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: Signs listed on the label include dizziness or light-headedness, sweating, shakiness, confusion or drowsiness, weakness, hunger, headache and a fast heartbeat.

visual.stock_query: icons of low blood sugar signs

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: If you notice those, follow the low blood sugar plan your care team gave you, and let your prescriber know.

scenes.section: When should you call your prescriber?
scenes.narration: And the slow-burn version. If tiredness isn't improving after a few weeks, or it's getting in the way of work, family or daily life, that's worth a call too. You don't need a crisis to ask.

visual.stock_query: warm phone call at kitchen table

scenes.narration: Let's pull it all together. If you're tired on tirzepatide, here's your checklist.
Small, regular meals, even when you're not hungry, with protein at each one.
Sip fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit them, and check that colour.
Protect your sleep, ease off caffeine gradually, and move a little, building toward strength work.

visual.stock_query: moon, cup and band with ticks

scenes.narration: Keep quick notes, and ask whether something else, like anaemia, diabetes, thyroid problems or sleep apnoea, could be playing a part.
And know your call-today signs: dehydration that isn't settling, dizziness or fainting, and low blood sugar signs if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea.
Remember Priya? She still has tired days. Everyone does. But now she knows what to check, what to ask, and when to call. That's the goal.
If you've been blaming yourself for feeling drained, please don't. Tiredness is a signal, not a character flaw. And now you know how to read it.
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The core claims all match their sources:
- **Label rates:** the Zepbound label (revised 8/2026) gives fatigue at 5%, 6% and 7% on 5, 10 and 15 mg vs 3% on placebo. This is pooled from SURMOUNT-1 and -2, 72 weeks each, and 5 mg was tested only in SURMOUNT-1. The label's fatigue term includes asthenia, fatigue, lethargy and malaise.
- **Label safety wording:** the sleep apnoea indication, the kidney/dehydration wording, the "may be higher" risk of low blood sugar with insulin or a sulfonylurea, and the list of low blood sugar signs all match.
- **NHS pages:** the self-help tips (meals every 3–4 h, 15-minute walk, mild dehydration, sleep routine, caffeine up to 7 h), the tiredness causes page (iron deficiency anaemia, diabetes, overactive thyroid, sleep apnoea, blood tests) and the dehydration page (symptoms, pale-pee check, urgent/111 and 999 criteria) all match.
- **CDC:** "7 or more hours" for adults 18–60.

The joint GLP-1 nutrition advisory (AJCN 2025, PMID 40450457) is confirmed via search and the Obesity Society page as recommending enough protein plus strength training to preserve lean mass. The "3+ times a week" figure matches the craft notes. I couldn't read the PDF text directly.

Framing is good throughout: absolute rates, the placebo comparison, "can, not proven", and the right population for sleep apnoea. Safety lines are complete: kidney-disease protein caveat, "unless told to limit fluids", low-blood-sugar warning for insulin/sulfonylurea users, the don't-stop line, the disclaimer and the prescriber line. The Priya scenario is clearly hypothetical.

There are four minor attribution and wording fixes below.

issues.claim: Ask whether blood tests, for example for anaemia, diabetes or thyroid problems, make sense for you / ask whether something else, like anaemia, diabetes, thyroid problems or sleep apnoea
issues.problem: The cited NHS page (S2) names an overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) specifically, both in its list of conditions and in its blood-test line. 'Thyroid problems' is broader than the source.
issues.fix: s59 narration: "So it's reasonable to ask your clinician whether blood tests, for example for anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid, make sense for you. That's their call to make with you, not a supplement aisle's." s77 narration: "Keep quick notes, and ask whether something else, like anaemia, diabetes, an overactive thyroid or sleep apnoea, could be playing a part."

issues.claim: The NHS says... If you want to cut back, do it gradually, because stopping suddenly can bring on headaches and trouble sleeping.
issues.problem: On the NHS page, the advice to cut back gradually is credited to The Sleep Charity, not the NHS itself. The way the sentence is built, the NHS gets credit for it.
issues.fix: Replace the last sentence with: "If you want to cut back, the NHS page points to advice from The Sleep Charity: do it gradually, because stopping suddenly can bring on headaches and trouble sleeping."

issues.claim: get an urgent GP appointment or call one-one-one
issues.problem: NHS 111 is UK-only, but most of the audience is in the US, Canada and Australia. US and Australian viewers have no 111 line to call.
issues.fix: Change the start to: "The NHS says to get an urgent appointment, in the UK that's your GP or one-one-one, elsewhere your doctor or local urgent care, if you feel unusually tired..." Keep the rest unchanged.

issues.claim: About seven reported fatigue or low energy.
issues.problem: 'Low energy' is a fair plain-English reading of the label's grouped term, but the script calls these numbers 'exactly as printed'. The label's fatigue term covers asthenia, fatigue, lethargy and malaise.
issues.fix: "About seven reported fatigue, weakness or low energy."

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are clean, legible designs with a single labelled battery mascot, brand colors and no text clutter. Candidate #0 uses the explicit worried→answered state-change layout (sleepy grey battery → smiling green battery) that the channel's own analytics show consistently outperforms big-number and reaction thumbnails at scale (Side Effects 4.04%, How Long 4.67%, Protein 3.78% vs. big-number 2.5-3.8% and reaction 2.1-2.9%).
